summary.text: 告 is used to tell, report, announce, inform, and accuse. Its ancient construction is disputed: proposals treat it as a mouth with a protruding tongue, or as 口 combined with an upper element identified as 牛 or abbreviated 壴.

formation.text: The graph’s formation is disputed. One analysis reads the whole graph as an open mouth with a protruding tongue; other analyses divide it into 口 and an upper element identified as 牛 or abbreviated 壴. The upper element’s identity and function remain unresolved.

components.text: In the mouth-and-tongue analysis, 口 depicts an open mouth. It also appears in the 牛-plus-mouth and 壴-plus-mouth analyses, though those accounts do not assign it a separate function.

history.text: The Shuowen explanation interprets 告 as an ox striking a person while a crossbar restrains its horns, thereby informing people, and analyzes the graph as 牛 plus 口. A later graphic account describes the seal form changing through clerical abbreviation and regular-script shaping into the modern form. This history of later forms does not confirm the parts of the earlier graph.
Uses are reported in oracle-bone, Western Zhou bronze, and Warring States materials. The cited examples do not establish a sequence of graphic forms or meanings.

uncertainties.text: The mouth-and-tongue, 牛-plus-mouth, and 壴-plus-mouth analyses compete; the early upper element is not securely identified.

A Southwestern Mandarin word meaning “try” or “check out” is proposed to have been written with 告 by borrowing the graph from 校. 告 and 校 are reported with similar Middle Chinese readings, but the borrowing direction and sound pathway remain uncertain.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone and later examples reported; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: An oracle-bone example concerning a deer report and later reporting or telling uses are cited. These attest reporting or telling uses but do not establish a single original meaning or a sequence of semantic change.

senses.period: Western Zhou examples reported; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Western Zhou bronze examples include reporting and admonishing uses. They do not establish when these uses arose or how they relate chronologically to earlier ones.

senses.period: Western Zhou examples reported; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: Accusatory use is reported among Western Zhou bronze examples; its relationship to “report” is not established.
Modern uses include telling, announcing, informing, and accusing. Their listing does not establish their chronology or semantic connections.

A Southwestern Mandarin word meaning “try” or “check out” is attested in a 1909 example. It is proposed that 告 borrowed the written sign from 校 for this similar-sounding word. The direction and sound pathway remain uncertain; this is not evidence that “tell” developed into “try”.

limitations.text: The cited examples do not establish a sequence connecting sacrificial, reporting, admonishing, accusatory, and telling uses.
The proposed borrowing from 校 lacks independent confirmation of its source account and historical sound pathway; similarity alone does not establish the direction of borrowing.

overview.text: 告 is used to tell and report. Its construction is disputed: proposals see an open mouth with a protruding tongue, or 口 combined with an upper element identified as 牛 or abbreviated 壴.

components.text: In one proposal, 口 depicts the mouth; the other accounts also include it with 牛 or 壴.

relationships.text: In the protruding-tongue analysis, 口 depicts the open mouth.
